A hash table stores key–value pairs so that a value can later be found quickly by its key. The central trick is to compute a small number from the key and use that number as an address into an array of buckets. Instead of searching every stored pair, the table jumps to one bucket and searches only what is there. When the distribution is good, that bucket contains very little, so the jump plus a short comparison is enough. The value might be a record, a count, or some other object; the lookup procedure is the same. The key is not discarded: it is stored beside its value, because the computed number is only a hint about where to look, not a unique identifier.

The number comes from a hash function, which turns a key such as a name, identifier, or string into an integer. A hash function should be deterministic—the same key must give same number every time—and fast to compute. It should also spread different keys across the available range as evenly as possible. The integer is then reduced, commonly by taking it modulo the number of buckets, to choose a bucket index. That reduction is simply a way of folding a large integer into the fixed range of available slots. If there are, say, one hundred buckets, the result is an index from zero through ninety-nine. A good hash function makes that bucket choice look almost arbitrary while still being repeatable.

Collisions are unavoidable. There are many possible keys and only a fixed number of buckets, so two or more different keys can be sent to the same bucket. Chaining handles this by letting each bucket hold a small collection, traditionally a linked list, of entries. Each entry stores the full key and its associated value. To insert a pair, the table hashes the key, goes to the chosen bucket, and adds the entry there. To look up a key, it hashes the key, follows the bucket index, and then walks through that bucket’s chain. At each entry it compares the stored key with the requested key; if they are equal, it returns the value. Because the search is by full key equality, two different keys that happen to land in the same bucket are not confused with one another. If the walk reaches the end without a match, the key is absent.

A small invented example makes the movement clear. Suppose the three keys cedar, maple, and pine are stored with their records, and suppose—purely for illustration, not because this describes any real hash function—that cedar hashes to bucket two, maple to bucket five, and pine to bucket two. The bucket for two therefore contains a chain with cedar and pine, while bucket five contains maple. A lookup for maple computes the invented hash, arrives at bucket five, compares maple with the key stored there, and immediately finds the matching value. A lookup for pine computes bucket two, enters the chain, compares its first key with pine; cedar does not match, so it moves to the next entry, where pine does match. Had it sought oak and the invented hash had sent oak to bucket five, it would check maple, see a different key, and conclude that oak was absent. These bucket numbers are made-up labels for the explanation, not a claim about how those words would really hash.

The load factor describes how crowded the table is. It is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. A table with eighty entries and one hundred buckets has a load factor of 0.8; on average, its chains are shorter than one item. As more entries arrive, the load factor rises and chains become longer, so lookups take more comparisons. To keep the average short, the table resizes when the load factor crosses a chosen threshold, perhaps three-quarters, though the exact choice is a matter of engineering. It allocates a larger bucket array—often roughly double the old size—and rehashes every stored key into the new array. This resizing is occasionally expensive, because every entry must be moved, but it happens rarely enough that its cost can be spread across many insertions. The point is to keep the load factor near a small constant.

This arrangement explains why hash-table lookup is expected to take constant time. Under a good, evenly distributing hash function and with the load factor held below a fixed bound, a key is likely to land in a bucket with only a small number of entries. The hash computation and bucket access are treated as constant-time steps, and the expected number of key comparisons does not grow with the total number of items. That expectation is an average over likely hash behavior; it is not a promise for every possible dataset or every single operation. If many keys collide in the same bucket, chaining degenerates into walking a long list. In the worst case, when all keys land in one bucket, finding an item can require checking every entry, which is linear time in the number of stored keys. A poor hash function, an unlucky set of keys, or keys deliberately chosen to collide can create that situation. Thus hash tables combine a fast expected case with a slower worst case, and good hash design and timely resizing are what keep the usual case close to the fast one. That is how the lookup finds its way.
